title: Nominal (C#) versus structural (JS/TS) typing
hook: C# asks whether two types share a name in the type system. JavaScript asks whether the object can satisfy the operation right now; TypeScript mostly follows structure unless you add brands or classes.

blocks.text: **Nominal typing** (C#, Java) declares compatibility by explicit type relationship — class, interface implementation, inheritance. **Structural typing** (TypeScript, Go interfaces) declares compatibility when required members exist. **JavaScript at runtime** is always structural duck typing with no static checker unless you add TS. Two unrelated C# classes with identical fields are **not** interchangeable; two JS objects with the same keys **are**.

entries.plainDefinition: Type compatibility requires named relationship — same class or declared interface.
entries.example: class Dog {} class Cat {} — neither assignable to the other though both empty.

entries.plainDefinition: If it has the members, it fits — no explicit implements required in TS.
entries.example: type Point = { x: number; y: number }; const p = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; // ok for Point

entries.plainDefinition: TS can merge interfaces — affects structural compatibility in advanced cases.
Both structural (shape) and nominal-ish (private/protected members) rules apply.
entries.example: Two classes with same public fields are not assignable if privates differ.

blocks.text: C# developers porting to TS assume `implements` matters at runtime — it does not. Refactors that rename a C# interface break compile; in JS the same JSON keeps working until someone removes a field. Conversely, TS structural rules allow **accidental compatibility** — two domain types with `{ id: string }` merge silently. Teams adopt **brands**, **readonly**, and **discriminated unions** to recover intent.

blocks.title: Interview trap: TS class instanceof
blocks.body: TS private fields make classes nominally incompatible at compile time, but runtime still uses prototype chain. instanceof checks prototype, not C#-style nominal identity for plain objects.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Expecting implements in TS to exist at runtime. Using as casts to silence structural errors. Porting C# DTO hierarchies verbatim without brands or discriminated unions. Confusing TS class private nominal rules with JS plain objects.

blocks.text: Architecture: use **discriminated unions** ({ kind: 'admin', ... }) for domain variants — structural but safe. For cross-service contracts, OpenAPI/Protobuf give nominal-like field IDs at the wire level while TS stays structural locally. When hiring C# devs onto TS monorepos, document that 'same shape' is not 'same type' until branded.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Stating TypeScript is object-oriented nominal like C#. Cannot explain excess property checking. Saying JS and TS typing models are identical — TS adds compile-time structural rules JS lacks.

interviewTakeaways: C# nominal: names and inheritance decide compatibility; JS runtime: shape only.
TypeScript is structural — extra literal properties can error; wider variables assign.
Recover intent with brands, discriminated unions, and runtime validation.
60s: C# nominal by name. TS structural by shape. JS runtime duck typing. JSON ignores all compile rules — validate at boundary.
Follow-up: MetricPoint vs ScreenPoint — how in TS vs C#?
commonPitfalls: Believing implements clauses exist in emitted JavaScript.
Using as casts to merge incompatible domain types.
Strong answer: three layers JS/TS/C#, structural vs nominal, brands and unions for safety.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Object literals get stricter structural checks than variables — surprises devs from nominal languages.
Closest runtime nominal check in JS — prototype-based, not name-based like C# types.
